# Malachi 4 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## Overview

Malachi 4 continues directly from Malachi 3:13–18 (in the Hebrew Bible there is no chapter division; Malachi 4:1–6 is numbered as Malachi 3:19–24). The chapter forms the conclusion not only of Malachi but of the entire Old Testament prophetic corpus. The prophet addresses the complaint of the discouraged faithful who saw the wicked prospering (Mal 3:14–15) by promising a coming day of decisive separation between righteous and wicked, closing with an admonition to remember the Law and a promise of Elijah's return.

---

## v. 1 — The Burning Day of Judgment

**Traditional Reading**

The "day" is the eschatological Day of the Lord. God compares it to a burning furnace — fire burns hotter in a furnace than in the open air (Hengstenberg, cited in Keil & Delitzsch). The "arrogant" and "every evildoer" point back to those described in Malachi 3:15 whom the people were calling "blessed." They will be like stubble (Hebrew *qash* — dry stalks or chaff) that a fire instantly consumes. "Neither root nor branch" is a metaphor from a tree signifying *total* destruction — no hope of sprouting again. This is not annihilationism but describes physical death and final judgment; the same metaphor appears in Amos 2:9.

- **EnduringWord (David Guzik)**: Notes the contrast between the *refining* fire for God's people (Mal 3:2–3) and the *burning* fire for the wicked. "Root nor branch" means no hope of recovery. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/)
- **JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown)**: The language is deliberately abrupt — "Behold, the day cometh! It burns like a furnace" — imparting terrible reality, as if the scene suddenly burst on the prophet's view. Primary fulfillment is the judgment on Jerusalem, but ultimate fulfillment is the day of general judgment. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/malachi-4.html)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: The "proud" (*zedim*) and "doer of wickedness" refer back to Mal 3:15. Those the people called blessed will be consumed. The subject of "will leave them" is the coming day itself. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)
- **Precept Austin (citing MacArthur)**: This is an eschatological Day of the Lord reference anticipating the return of Christ in judgment (cf. Rev 19:11–21). The Day of the Lord is mentioned four times in Malachi's closing verses (3:17; 4:1, 3, 5). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_4_commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_4_commentary)
- **Clarke (Methodist/Wesleyan)**: Sees the primary fulfillment as the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans in AD 70. "Neither root nor branch" is a proverbial expression for total destruction — neither man nor child escapes. [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/malachi/4.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/malachi/4.htm)
- **Constable (Dispensational)**: "All the arrogant and every evildoer" is a hendiadys meaning "every arrogant evildoer." The judgment of wicked unbelievers is in view (cf. Matt 25:46), ultimately fulfilled at the end of the Millennium (Rev 20:11–15). He explicitly states this verse gives no basis for annihilationism. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html)

---

## v. 2 — The Sun of Righteousness

**Traditional Reading**

In stark contrast to the furnace awaiting the wicked, those who "fear My name" (echoing Mal 3:16) will experience the rising of the "Sun of Righteousness." The "wings" are the sun's rays or sunbeams spreading over the earth. "Healing" (*marpe*) signifies spiritual restoration and wholeness. The righteous are pictured as stall-fed calves released to pasture — leaping, frisking, and full of joy. The imagery speaks of liberation, joy, and prosperity.

**Major Interpretive Divide: Is "Sun of Righteousness" a Messianic title?**

This is the most debated phrase in the chapter:

- **Messianic/Personal View (traditional Christian, from Justin Martyr onward)**: "Sun of Righteousness" is a title for Jesus Christ. Just as God is called a "sun" in Psalm 84:11 and the New Jerusalem has no need of the sun because God's glory illuminates it (Rev 21:23), so Christ is the Sun who brings righteousness and healing.
    - **EnduringWord (Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic)**: "From the time of early Christians like Justin Martyr to today, Christians have regarded the Sun of Righteousness as a reference to Jesus." The "wings" are the rays or sunbeams bringing healing. "Imagine trying to light a candle on a sunny day to help out the sun! That makes as much sense as trying to 'improve' the work of Jesus for us with our own righteousness." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/)
    - **Clarke (Methodist)**: "The Sun of righteousness — The Lord Jesus, the promised Messiah; the Hope of Israel." [https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/malachi/4.htm](https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/malachi/4.htm)
    - **JFB (Reformed)**: The spiritual blessings brought by Christ are summed up in "righteousness" (1 Cor 1:30) and spiritual "healing" (Psalm 103:3). The wings imply the winged swiftness with which He shall appear. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/malachi-4.html)
    - **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: "The Sun of righteousness (the Christ, anointed one) would arise." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/malachi-4.html)
    - **GotQuestions.org (Evangelical)**: "The 'Sun of Righteousness' is an unmistakable reference to the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Light of the world (John 9:5)." This healing goes beyond physical to spiritual restoration. [https://www.gotquestions.org/healing-in-His-wings.html](https://www.gotquestions.org/healing-in-His-wings.html)

- **Non-Personal/Age-of-Blessing View**: "Sun of Righteousness" is not a personal title for the Messiah but a metaphor for the righteous, healing age that God will inaugurate.
    - **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran/Reformed scholarship)**: "By the sun of righteousness the fathers, from Justin downwards, and nearly all the earlier commentators understand Christ ... But in the verse before us the context does not sustain the personal view, but simply the idea that righteousness *itself* is regarded as a sun." *Tsedaqah* is not justification/forgiveness (there is no forgiving of sins *on* the day of judgment), but righteousness in its consequences — the sum and substance of salvation. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)
    - **Constable (Dispensational)**: "Some expositors have understood 'the sun of righteousness' to be a messianic title, but it seems best to view it as a description of the day of blessing that Messiah will bring, the Millennium. The New Testament never referred to Jesus Christ as 'the sun of righteousness.'" [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html)
    - **Utley (Baptist)**: Notes the KJV and NKJV capitalize "Sun," but "this is exegetically impossible because it is a FEMININE NOUN in this context (it is usually MASCULINE)." It is "a unique reference to the Messiah" in traditional understanding, but contextually seems to be "a metaphor inaugurating the new age of restoration." He also notes a possible Zoroastrian background — the Persian high god's symbol was a winged sun disk. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html)
    - **Peake's Commentary (Modern Scholarship)**: "Malachi is not definitely predicting Christ, or indeed any personal agent." Notes the Babylonian sun-god Shamash was conceived as god of justice, and Assyrian, Persian, and Egyptian monuments depict the solar disc with wings. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/malachi-4.html)

**The "Calves from the Stall"**

All traditions agree on the joyful imagery. **Spurgeon** (cited in EnduringWord): "The calf in the stall is shut up, tied up with a halter at night, but when the sun rises the calf goes forth to the pasture ... So the child of God may be in bondage. The recollection of past sins and present unbelief may halter him up and keep him in the stall, but when the Lord reveals himself he is set free." **Calvin** rendered it "leap" as frisking calves. The **Vulgate** has *salietis* ("you shall leap"); the **LXX** has *skirtēsate hōs moscharia ek desmōn aneimena* ("you shall bound as calves set free from restraints"). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/); [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/malachi-4.html)

---

## v. 3 — Trampling the Wicked

**Traditional Reading**

The righteous will trample the wicked, who have become "ashes" — the residue of the burning judgment of v. 1. The imagery may derive from the winepress (treading down) or from military victory (cf. Joshua 10:24, where defeated kings are placed under feet). This is eschatological vindication: the apparent prosperity of the wicked (the complaint of Mal 3:15) is completely reversed.

- **JFB**: The righteous shall be the army attending Christ in His final destruction of the ungodly (cf. 1 Cor 6:2; Rev 2:26–27; 19:14–15). "Ashes" — after having been burnt with the fire of judgment. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/malachi-4.html)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: Those who fear God will "acquire power over the ungodly" — they will tread down the wicked who have become ashes, lying like ashes on the ground. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)
- **Utley**: "This is a metaphor from the wine press, which is used for the righteous finally overcoming ... Notice God's victory is not immediate, but eschatological." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html)
- **Layman's Bible Commentary**: Malachi's idea that righteous Jews will turn against their fellow Jews "is not found elsewhere in the Old Testament." Christians later reinterpreted this participation in judgment through missionary activity and the Last Judgment. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/malachi-4.html)

---

## v. 4 — Remember the Law of Moses

**Traditional Reading**

After prophesying the coming day, the prophet (and God through him) commands the people to "remember the Law of Moses." This is not salvation by works but a call to covenant faithfulness while they wait. The mention of "Horeb" (the Deuteronomic name for Sinai) and "statutes and ordinances" echoes Deuteronomy's language. After Malachi, God's prophetic voice would be silent for roughly 400 years — they needed to live by what they already had.

- **EnduringWord (Guzik)**: "Malachi warns Israel to remember the Law because God's prophetic voice would be silent for some 400 years. We never need to despair when God seems silent, because what He has already said is rich enough." Notes that under the old covenant, man related to God on the basis of law — "the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17)." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: The admonition forms the conclusion of the whole book, not just the last section. It is a "perfectly general admonition to lay to heart and observe the law ... not according to its casual and transient form, but according to its real essence as expressing the holiness of God, just as in Matthew 5:17." "My servant" traces the law back to God as its author. The whole admonition forms an antithesis to the rebuke that from the days of their fathers they went away from God's ordinances. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)
- **Constable**: "Moses' last words to the Israelites in Deuteronomy contain about 14 exhortations to remember the Law ... Malachi closed his book, and God closed the Old Testament, with the same exhortation." Nine connections between Malachi and Deuteronomy have been identified. Malachi "begins by pointing to the past and ends by pointing to the future, thus appropriately grounding the ethical impact of the book in both redemption and eschatology." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html)
- **Precept Austin**: *Zakar* (remember) means not only to be reminded but also to act accordingly — to be hearers *and* doers of the Word. "The doing of the Law in no way saved them but" was the expected response of the redeemed. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_4_commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/malachi_4_commentary)
- **Expositor's Bible Commentary**: "With his last word the prophet significantly calls upon the people to remember the Law. This is their one hope before the coming of the great and terrible day of the Lord." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/malachi-4.html)

---

## vv. 5–6 — Elijah the Prophet and the Turning of Hearts

**Traditional Reading**

God promises to send "Elijah the prophet" before the great and terrible Day of the Lord. His mission: to turn the hearts of fathers to children and children to fathers, lest God come and strike the land with a curse (*cherem* — the ban, total destruction). This is the final promise of the Old Testament.

**Who Is This Elijah?**

All Christian traditions connect this promise to John the Baptist, but they differ on whether John *fully* or only *partially* fulfilled it:

- **Full Fulfillment in John the Baptist**:
    - **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran/Reformed)**: John the Baptist *is* the promised Elijah. The angel Gabriel announced him as going before the Lord "in the spirit and power of Elijah" (Luke 1:17). Jesus said "Elijah has already come" (Matt 17:12). John's denial in John 1:21 was a denial of being Elijah *reincarnated*, which was the Jewish expectation. The prophecy was not merely "provisional" — "the prophets of the Old Testament throughout make no allusion to any second coming of the Lord to His people." The Day of the Lord *commenced* with Christ's first coming and the judgment that followed (destruction of Jerusalem, AD 70). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)

- **Partial Fulfillment in John, Complete Fulfillment in a Future Elijah**:
    - **EnduringWord (Guzik, Pentecostal/Charismatic)**: John fulfilled it "in a figurative sense" (Matt 11:14; Mark 9:11–13; Luke 1:17). "Yet because this Elijah comes before the coming of the great and dreadful day, we know that the Elijah prophecy is only completely fulfilled just before the second coming of Jesus." Points to Matt 17:11–12 and Rev 11:3–12 (the two witnesses) as evidence of a future fulfillment. Also notes the Jewish Passover tradition of setting a place for Elijah. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/)
    - **Constable (Dispensational)**: John *would have been* the Elijah if the people had accepted Jesus as Messiah (Matt 11:14). "Since they did not, John did not fulfill this prophecy about Elijah coming, though he did fulfill the prophecy about Messiah's forerunner (Mal 3:1)." Jesus' post-Transfiguration words (Matt 17:11, after John's death) say Elijah "will come and restore all things" — indicating a future fulfillment. Constable suggests the two witnesses of Rev 11 will carry out this ministry. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html)
    - **Dummelow's Commentary**: "Malachi's meaning would be clearer if we were to translate, with a slight concession to English idiom, 'I will send you a prophet Elijah': cp. 'a Daniel come to judgment.'" Notes that "whenever 'the old order changes, giving place to new,' God sends the world an Elijah." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/malachi-4.html)

**What Does "Turning Hearts" Mean?**

- **Keil & Delitzsch**: It is not about settling family disputes. "The fathers are ... the ancestors of the Israelitish nation, the patriarchs, and generally the pious forefathers ... The sons or children are the degenerate descendants of Malachi's own time." The hearts of godly fathers and ungodly sons are estranged because common love to God is missing. Elijah will "restore the heart of the fathers, in the sons, or give to the sons the fathers' disposition and affections." Luke 1:17's paraphrase — "the unbelieving to the wisdom of the just" — provides the authoritative explanation. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)
- **EnduringWord (Guzik)**: "This promise speaks of more than the reconciliation of families. When God turns the hearts of the children to their fathers, it also has in mind turning to the God of their fathers; to the faith of the patriarchs." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/)
- **Utley (Baptist)**: The Hebrew verb (*shuv*, "turn" or "turn back") has a double focus: (1) return the post-exilic community to the faith of their fathers; (2) return stability to the family structure of the faith community. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html)
- **Constable**: At Christ's first coming, He brought family division (Matt 10:35–36); at the end, the Elijah figure will unite Jewish families in faith. If this turning does not happen, the land would be struck with a curse — but "because the Jews will turn to Jesus Christ in faith (Zech 12:10), blessing will come to the earth, not a curse (cf. Zech 14:11; Rom 11:26)." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/malachi-4.html)

**The Curse Ending**

- **EnduringWord**: The Masoretes (traditional Hebrew scribes) were so bothered by the Old Testament ending with "curse" that they repeated the next-to-last verse after the last verse. Similarly, the Septuagint (LXX) reverses the last two verses so the OT ends with a blessing, not a curse. The NT ends differently: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all!" (Rev 22:21). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/)
- **Keil & Delitzsch (footnote)**: Confirms the LXX put Mal 4:4 at the end "not to call attention to its great importance, but probably for the very same reason for which the Masora observes ... that in the books of Isaiah, the twelve prophets, the Lamentations, and Ecclesiastes, the last verse but one of these books was to be repeated when they were read in the synagogue, namely, because the last verse had too harsh a sound." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)
- **Utley**: *Cherem* (the ban/curse) is "the term which is used of something being dedicated to God, and it becoming so holy that it must be completely destroyed" (cf. Lev 27:28–29; Josh 6:17). It recalls the fate of the Canaanites. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/malachi-4.html)

**Moses and Elijah Together**

- **EnduringWord**: Significant that the closing words of the OT refer to both Moses and Elijah. Both met God at Mount Sinai/Horeb (Exod 3:1; 1 Kgs 19:8–18). Both met Jesus at the Mount of Transfiguration (Matt 17:1–5). They are probably the two witnesses of Revelation 11. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/malachi-4/)
- **Keil & Delitzsch**: "Upon the Mount of Christ's Transfiguration, therefore, there appeared both Moses, the founder of the law and mediator of the old covenant, and Elijah the prophet, as the restorer of the law in Israel, to talk with Jesus of His decease which He was to accomplish in Jerusalem." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/malachi-4.html)

---

## Summary of Key Tradition Differences

| Issue | Traditional Christian / Evangelical / Pentecostal | Keil & Delitzsch / Some Reformed | Dispensational |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Sun of Righteousness" | Messianic title for Jesus (Justin Martyr, Clarke, Guzik, JFB, GotQuestions) | Not personal — righteousness itself as a sun bringing salvation; context does not support a personal Christological reading | Not a Messianic title; describes the Millennial age of blessing |
| Elijah fulfillment | John the Baptist fulfilled it (most) | John the Baptist is the complete fulfillment; no second fulfillment needed | John fulfilled it only partially; a future Elijah-figure (possibly one of the two witnesses) will complete it before the Second Coming |
| Day of the Lord | Both near-historical and final eschatological judgment | Commenced with Christ's first coming; judgment unfolded in AD 70; continues through church age to final judgment | Strictly eschatological, associated with the Tribulation and Second Coming |

**Note on Catholic and Orthodox readings**: Specific Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) and Orthodox (oca.org) search results were not obtainable within the available searches. However, Keil & Delitzsch notes that the "fathers and Catholic commentators" generally held that the Elijah prophecy would be fulfilled in the actual reappearance of the risen Elijah before Christ's second coming — a view K&D disputes. The traditional Catholic reading of "Sun of Righteousness" as a Messianic title aligns with the broader Christian tradition going back to Justin Martyr. The LXX (Septuagint), which is the Old Testament of the Orthodox Church, transposes the final verses so Malachi ends with "Remember the law of Moses" rather than "curse."

**Note on prosperity/Word of Faith readings**: No specific results were found from approved sites addressing a distinct prosperity-gospel reading of Malachi 4. However, EnduringWord (David Guzik) applies v. 2 devotionally — "They shall grow fat — growing strong and prosperous in the LORD" — which some traditions might emphasize in terms of material blessing. Guzik connects this to spiritual prosperity and joy in Christ rather than wealth.
